2027-03-26.title: Friday of the Passion of the Lord (Good Friday)
readings: He was wounded for our transgressions
Father, into your hands I commend my spirit
He learned obedience and became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him
The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to John
2027-03-26.alt: Good Friday. No Mass is celebrated today or tomorrow until the Easter Vigil. The Celebration of the Lord's Passion takes place in the afternoon, ideally about three o'clock: Liturgy of the Word with the Solemn Intercessions, Adoration of the Holy Cross, Holy Communion. The altar is completely bare, without cross, candles or cloths. Day of fasting and abstinence (abstinence from meat from age 14; fasting, one full meal, from 18 to 59; follow the norms of your diocese). The Collection for the Holy Land is taken up today. The Divine Mercy Novena begins today. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-03-26.verse: When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
theo: Today the Church does not celebrate Mass. The tabernacle stands open and empty, the altar is stripped bare, the bells are silent. On this one day of the year the Church gathers not to offer the sacrifice in sacramental form but to stand at the foot of the Cross where it was offered once for all. The first reading is the fourth Song of the Suffering Servant, written centuries before Christ: a man “despised and rejected by others; a man of suffering and acquainted with infirmity,” who goes silent “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter.” And the prophet tells us why: “he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed.” The Church has always read this song as the clearest picture of Good Friday in the whole Old Testament. The Psalm puts on our lips the words Jesus himself prayed on the cross in St Luke's Gospel: “Into your hand I commit my spirit.”

The Letter to the Hebrews shows us who is suffering. He is “a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God,” and yet he is not distant from us: “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who in every respect has been tested as we are, yet without sin.” In the days of his flesh he “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears,” and “although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.” That obedience, carried to the end, makes him “the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him.” So the reading ends with an invitation that fits this afternoon exactly: “Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness.” The Cross is that throne of grace.

Then we hear the Passion according to St John, read every Good Friday. John shows Jesus not as a victim dragged along but as the King who goes freely to his throne. In the garden across the Kidron he steps forward and asks: “Whom are you looking for?” When he answers “I am he,” the soldiers step back and fall to the ground. He heals the ear Peter has cut, and he goes with them. Before Annas he speaks openly; Peter, warming himself at the charcoal fire, denies him three times. Before Pilate he speaks of a kingdom “not from this world” and of the truth, and Pilate asks: “What is truth?” He is scourged, crowned with thorns, clothed in purple, and shown to the crowd: “Here is the man!” Carrying the cross by himself, he goes out to Golgotha. Over his head Pilate writes in Hebrew, Latin and Greek: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” The soldiers cast lots for his seamless tunic. From the cross he gives his mother to the beloved disciple and the disciple to his mother. He says “I am thirsty,” receives the sour wine on a branch of hyssop, and says: “It is finished.” Then he bows his head and hands over his spirit. A soldier pierces his side, and at once blood and water flow out. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bind his body with spices and lay it in a new tomb in a garden.

Who is responsible for this death? The Church answers clearly. It is not “the Jews” of then, nor the Jewish people of today: the Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in the Passion “cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today” (Nostra Aetate 4). When St John writes “the Jews,” he usually means the Temple authorities of that time; Jesus, his mother and all the Apostles were Jews. The Catechism says that all sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion, and that we Christians bear the heavier responsibility when we crucify him again by our sins (Catechism 597–598). So we do not point a finger today. We strike our breast. And we discover that the Cross is not first of all a crime but a gift: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). Love has gone to the end. “It is finished” is not a cry of defeat but the word of a work completed: the Father's will done, the Scriptures fulfilled, the world redeemed.
conn: How the liturgy unfolds (1): entrance in silence.

The priest and deacon, in red vestments, go to the bare altar in silence, without song. They prostrate themselves on the floor (or kneel), and everyone kneels and prays in silence. Then the priest says the opening prayer, without “Let us pray”.
(2) The Liturgy of the Word.

Isaiah 52–53, Psalm 31, Hebrews 4–5, then the Passion according to John, often read in parts by three readers. Candles and incense are not used for the Gospel. At the words “he gave up his spirit” all kneel and pause in silence. A short homily may follow.
(3) The Solemn Intercessions.

Ten great prayers for the whole world: for the Church, the Pope, all orders of the faithful, catechumens, the unity of Christians, the Jewish people, those who do not believe in Christ, those who do not believe in God, those in public office, and those in tribulation. For each, the deacon announces the intention, all pray in silence (they may kneel and rise), and the priest sings the prayer.
(4) The Adoration of the Cross.

The Cross is shown in one of two ways: either it is unveiled in three stages, or it is carried in procession from the church door with three stops. Each time the priest sings: “Behold the wood of the Cross, on which hung the salvation of the world,” and all answer: “Come, let us adore,” and kneel in silence. Then the people come forward one by one and venerate the Cross with a genuflection, a kiss or another sign of reverence, while the Reproaches (“My people, what have I done to you?”) and other hymns are sung.
(5) Holy Communion.

A cloth, corporal and the Missal are placed on the altar. The Blessed Sacrament, consecrated at yesterday's Mass of the Lord's Supper, is brought from the place of repose by the shortest way, with candles. All say the Our Father; the faithful receive Communion. There is no consecration today.
(6) Departure in silence.

After the prayer after Communion, the priest prays over the people with hands outstretched. There is no final blessing in the usual form and no dismissal: all leave in silence. The altar is stripped again; the Cross remains with candles for private veneration.
Why no Mass?

From the earliest centuries the Church has refrained from celebrating the Eucharist on Good Friday and Holy Saturday. The Sacrifice is present today not on the altar but on the Cross itself, which we contemplate and adore.
“The Jews” in John.

In John the term usually refers to the Temple authorities who opposed Jesus, not to the whole people. The Church forbids any use of the Passion to blame the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597).
Gabbatha and Golgotha.
Gabbatha (the Stone Pavement) was the place of judgement; Golgotha (the place of the skull) a rocky height outside the city wall, today within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
Hyssop and the Lamb.

A branch of hyssop was used to mark the doorposts with the blood of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:22). John notes that the legs of Jesus were not broken, as with the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46): he is the true Lamb.
altar: There is no Mass today, yet we receive Communion from the hosts consecrated at the Lord's Supper. The Body given on the cross and the Body given at the table are one and the same: the one Sacrifice of Christ.
Every Mass makes present this Sacrifice of Calvary in an unbloody manner. Good Friday teaches us what we receive at every altar: the Body that was given up and the Blood that was poured out for us.
outline: Point to the bare altar and the empty tabernacle, and ask: why is the church so empty today?
Point 1 · The Servant wounded for us
Isaiah's fourth Song: by his bruises we are healed.
Point 2 · The King on the Cross
John's Passion: free, majestic, truthful to the end.
Blood and water from his side: the sacraments and the Church.
Point 4 · The high priest who sympathizes
Approach the throne of grace with boldness.
People in a long line waiting to kiss a wooden cross.
“Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.”
live: Eat one simple meal, no meat; offer the hunger for those who suffer, and give what you save to the Holy Land collection or the poor.
At three in the afternoon, stop for a few minutes of silence wherever you are, or join the Celebration of the Lord's Passion.
Make the Way of the Cross
Walk the fourteen stations in church or at home with your family.
When you venerate the Cross, name one person you need to forgive, and forgive them there.
fathers: Blood and water flowed from his side: water for Baptism and blood for the Eucharist. As Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, so the Church was formed from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross.
He hung on the cross, and the cross became a teacher's chair. From it he taught us how to love: he prayed for his persecutors and gave his mother into the care of his disciple.

Had there been no cross, Christ would not have been crucified; had there been no crucifixion, life would not have been nailed to the tree; and death would not have been trampled underfoot. The cross is the trophy of our salvation.
magis: The trial of Jesus; the Jewish people are not collectively responsible for his death; all sinners were the authors of his Passion.
The redemptive death of Christ: “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures”; the Lamb of God; the Cross as the unique sacrifice.
The Second Vatican Council on the Church and the Jewish people.
The Congregation for Divine Worship (1988) on the celebration of Good Friday.
Good Friday, like Ash Wednesday, is a day of fasting and abstinence.
saints: Begins today and continues until the Saturday before the Second Sunday of Easter (Divine Mercy Sunday, 4 April 2027).

27 Mar: Holy Saturday; Easter Vigil after nightfall. 28 Mar: Easter Sunday of the Resurrection of the Lord. 29 Mar–3 Apr: the Octave of Easter. 4 Apr: Second Sunday of Easter (Divine Mercy). The Annunciation of the Lord, which fell on Holy Thursday, is transferred to Monday 5 April 2027.
2027-03-26.prayer: Remember your mercies, O Lord, and with your eternal protection sanctify your servants, for whom Christ your Son, by the shedding of his Blood, established the Paschal Mystery. Who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, King on the Cross, by your wounds we are healed. We adore you and we bless you, because by your holy Cross you have redeemed the world. Let the blood and water from your side wash us and feed us, keep us near your Mother at the foot of the Cross, and bring us with you to the joy of Easter. Amen.

quick: The Suffering Servant was wounded for our sins; by his bruises we are healed.
In John's Passion Jesus goes freely to the Cross as King and dies saying: It is finished.
We adore the Cross, the throne of grace, and receive Communion; there is no Mass today.
2027-03-26.action: Keep the fast and abstinence, and at three o'clock stop for five minutes of silence before a crucifix.
2027-03-26.question: What does it mean for me that he was wounded for my transgressions?
catechism: Who is responsible for the death of Jesus: all sinners.
The death of Christ is the unique and definitive sacrifice.
The love of Christ “to the end” gives his sacrifice its value.
kidsaint: The Good Thief (St Dismas, by tradition)

Jesus was crucified between two thieves. One of them said: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. Jesus promised him: today you will be with me in Paradise. Lesson: it is never too late to say sorry to Jesus.
2027-03-26.special: Good Friday of the Passion of the Lord: no Mass; Celebration of the Lord's Passion; fasting and abstinence; Collection for the Holy Land.
term: The central rite of Good Friday: the Cross is shown with the chant “Behold the wood of the Cross,” and each person comes forward to genuflect before it or kiss it. We do not worship wood; we adore Christ who saved us on it.

family.explain: Jesus was dying on the cross, and his mother Mary stood near him with John. Even then Jesus thought of others: he gave Mary to John as his mother, and John to Mary as her son. Then he said: It is finished. He had loved us all the way to the end.
family.intention: We pray for everyone who suffers today, and for all who will be baptized at Easter.
family.ask: Ask: “What can our family do today to remember how much Jesus loves us?” (For example: silence at three o'clock, a simple meal, the Way of the Cross.)

illus: In a Latin parish near Kollam, an old fisherman always came early on Good Friday and stood near the back. When the line formed to kiss the Cross, he waited until everyone else had gone. Asked why, he said: the sea has taken many things from me, and I have said hard words to God because of it. I come last so that I can stay longer at his feet and tell him I am sorry. Then I go home lighter.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, we adore you and we bless you, because by your holy Cross you have redeemed the world. Amen.
share: He was wounded for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5). Which of my sins do I see in his wounds?
Here is your mother (John 19:27). Do I take Mary into my home as the beloved disciple did?
Let us approach the throne of grace with boldness (Hebrews 4:16). What do I need to bring to the Cross today?
pm.resp: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.
interc: For the holy Church, that God may keep her in peace and unity.
For the Jewish people, the first to hear the word of God, that they may continue to grow in faithfulness to his covenant.
For all Christians, that we may be gathered into one at the foot of the Cross.
For the sick, the dying, prisoners and refugees, that they may find strength in the crucified Lord.
For our group, that we may never be ashamed of the Cross of Christ.
pm.close: Father, you did not spare your own Son but gave him up for us all. Through his Cross bring us to the glory of his Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, look at our church today. The altar is bare. The tabernacle is empty and its door stands open. There are no flowers, no bells, no Mass. Everything is stripped away so that only one thing remains: the Cross. Today we stand where Mary stood, at the foot of the Cross.

Seven hundred years before Christ, Isaiah saw him: he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). Like a lamb led to the slaughter, he did not open his mouth. When we look at the crucifix, we must say: that is what my sin cost. And that is how much I am loved.

St John shows us that Jesus is not a helpless victim. In the garden he steps forward: whom are you looking for? I am he. Before Pilate he speaks of the truth. He carries his own cross. Above his head is written: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. The Cross is his throne. He reigns by giving his life.

Who killed Jesus? Not a people. The Church teaches that we must never blame the Jewish people for his death. All sinners caused his Passion; I did, you did (Catechism 598). So today we do not point at others. We strike our own breast. And we hear him say from the cross: Father, forgive them.

From the cross he gives us his mother: here is your mother (John 19:27). Then he says: it is finished, bows his head and hands over his spirit (John 19:30). The soldier's spear opens his side, and blood and water flow: the Eucharist and Baptism, the Church born from the heart of Christ.

Soon we will come forward to adore the Cross. As you bend to kiss it, give him your sins, your sorrows and your dead. He is the high priest who sympathizes with our weakness. Let us approach the throne of grace with boldness (Hebrews 4:16). We adore you, O Christ, and we bless you, because by your holy Cross you have redeemed the world. Amen.
kids: Children, today the church is very quiet and the altar is bare, because we remember that Jesus died on the cross for us. He loved us so much that he gave his whole life.
When you kiss the cross today, say in your heart: thank you, Jesus. I love you. I am sorry for my sins.

opts.a: He learned obedience through what he suffered
intro: The Letter to the Hebrews shows us the inner Passion of Jesus: his prayers, his tears and his obedience. Today we look into the heart of our High Priest.

points.apply: Bring your tears to the Cross today in prayer.

sub: The Son's yes to the Father.
points.apply: In one hard thing this week, say: Father, your will be done.
Approach Jesus with confidence; kiss the Cross with trust.

concl: Jesus prayed, wept and obeyed; and through his suffering he became our salvation.
Our High Priest knows our weakness and opens the way to mercy.
opts.resolve: Today I will bring my tears to the Cross and say, with Jesus, Father, your will be done.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the Gospel of John shows us Jesus as King on the Cross. The Letter to the Hebrews lets us look inside his heart. In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission (Hebrews 5:7).

Loud cries and tears. The Son of God was not ashamed to weep. In Gethsemane he fell to the ground. On the Cross he cried out. And Hebrews says: he was heard. But he still died. How was he heard? The Father did not take him out of death; he brought him through death into the Resurrection. Psalm 22 says: he did not hide his face from me, but heard when I cried to him (Psalm 22:24). God hears our cries too, even when the answer comes on the other side of the cross.

Then comes a mysterious sentence: although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered (Hebrews 5:8). Jesus was always obedient. But in his human nature he lived that obedience through pain, step by step, to the end. Isaiah had said of the Servant: I was not rebellious, I did not turn backward (Isaiah 50:5). The disobedience of Adam is undone by the obedience of Christ.

And having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him (Hebrews 5:9). The Cross is not only a place of suffering; it is a fountain. Out of his anguish he shall see light, says Isaiah (Isaiah 53:11). And because he has suffered, we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

So when you come forward to venerate the Cross, bring your tears. Bring the prayers that seem unanswered. Bring the hard obedience God is asking of you. Kneel before the One who prayed with loud cries, and say with him: Father, not my will but yours. He will hear you, as the Father heard him. Amen.

opts.a: They will look on the one whom they have pierced
intro: John's Passion is full of small details that fulfil the Scriptures: the thirst of Jesus, his seamless tunic, his pierced side. Each detail speaks to us today.

points.apply: Give someone thirsty a drink this week, and give Jesus your love.

sub: The soldiers do not tear it.
points.apply: Pray for Christian unity and heal one division in your family or parish.

sub: The spear and the open side.
points.apply: Spend five minutes today simply looking at a crucifix.

concl: In the small details of the Passion, Scripture is fulfilled and love is revealed.
Today we look on the One we pierced, and we find mercy.
opts.resolve: Today I will look on the crucifix with love, quench his thirst by my love, and work for unity.
homily: Dear friends, St John wrote his Passion with great care. Again and again he tells us: this was to fulfil the scripture. Today let us look at three small details, and let them speak to our hearts.

First, Jesus' thirst. When Jesus knew that all was now finished, he said (in order to fulfill the scripture), “I am thirsty” (John 19:28). The One through whom all rivers were made now thirsts on a cross. The psalm had said: for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink (Psalm 69:21). St Teresa of Calcutta had the words I thirst written beside the crucifix in every chapel of her sisters. Jesus thirsts not only for water but for our love, for souls. Each time we serve the poor, we give him to drink.

Second, his tunic. The soldiers divided his clothes, but the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top. So they said: let us not tear it, but cast lots for it (John 19:23–24). The psalm had foretold it: for my clothing they cast lots (Psalm 22:18). The Fathers of the Church saw in that seamless garment the unity of the Church. Even the soldiers did not tear it. Shall we, his disciples, tear his Church apart by quarrels and divisions?

Third, his side. One of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out. And John adds: they will look on the one whom they have pierced (John 19:37). Zechariah had prophesied: when they look on the one whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child (Zechariah 12:10). Today the whole Church looks on him, and mourns, and is healed.

So today, look. Look long at the crucifix. Let his thirst move you to love. Let his seamless tunic call you to unity. Let his open side draw you into his mercy. And when you kneel to venerate the Cross, say simply: Lord, I look on you whom I have pierced; have mercy on me. Amen.

intro: The Servant wounded for us, the King on the Cross, the fountain from his side, and the high priest who sympathizes with our weakness.

sub: By his bruises we are healed.
q: But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the cross, so that, free from sins, we might live for righteousness; by his wounds you have been healed.
points.apply: Look at a crucifix for five minutes today and say slowly: for me.

sub: A kingdom not from this world.
q: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, from the words of my groaning?
Pilate also had an inscription written and put on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”
points.apply: Pray Psalm 22 today, the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross, from beginning to end.

points.h: It is finished: the fountain from his side
sub: The Church born from his heart.
q: On that day a fountain shall be opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and impurity.
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.
points.apply: Thank God today for your Baptism and for every Communion you have received.

sub: Tested as we are, yet without sin.
q: Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our diseases; yet we accounted him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted.

For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who in every respect has been tested as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
points.apply: Bring one burden to the Cross today and leave it there; and visit or call someone who is suffering.

concl: The Cross is not defeat but love completed: the Servant, the King and the Priest give their life for us.
No one people is to blame; all sinners caused his Passion, and all are invited to his mercy.
2027-03-26.resolve: Keep the fast, adore the Cross, and forgive one person from the heart today.
